summary:
P.U.L.S.E. (Personal Unified Life Support Evaluator) is an autonomous, AI-driven health monitoring and closed-loop life support system designed for deep-space exploration.
What we developed:
We designed an end-to-end aerospace architecture and an interactive Edge AI web prototype. The system integrates non-invasive spacesuit biosensors—smart silver-threaded ECG textiles, optical SpO₂ sensors, and microfluidic sweat patches—with predictive time-series neural networks calibrated using real historical EVA telemetry from NASA’s Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) and Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).
How it solves the problem:
In deep space, communication delays with Earth reach up to 20 minutes one way, making real-time flight surgeon intervention impossible during emergencies. P.U.L.S.E. processes biometrics locally with zero latency, predicts critical events like heat exhaustion or hypoxia up to 20 minutes before onset, and automatically adjusts spacesuit cooling and oxygen flow via a Closed-Loop ECLSS interface.
Why it matters:
P.U.L.S.E. ensures crew survival during autonomous Lunar and Martian missions while offering immediate dual-use impact on Earth for firefighters, underground miners, and remote telemedicine.
details: What It Does & How It Works P.U.L.S.E. (Personal Unified Life Support Evaluator) is an autonomous, AI-driven astronaut health monitoring and closed-loop life support system designed for deep-space exploration. 1. Non-Invasive Biosensing: It integrates smart silver-threaded ECG textiles, forehead optical SpO₂ sensors, and microfluidic sweat patches to track hydration, electrolytes, and stress hormones in real time. 2. Local Edge AI & NASA Data Calibration: Instead of relying on delayed Earth communications, an onboard Edge AI processor analyzes biometric time-series locally. Our predictive models (LSTM & Sensor Fusion) are calibrated against historical EVA physiological baselines from NASA’s Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) and Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). 3. Closed-Loop Response: When P.U.L.S.E. detects early anomalies (predicting heat stress or hypoxia up to 18–20 minutes before symptoms appear), it alerts the astronaut via their helmet HUD and automatically commands the spacesuit’s Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) to adjust cooling and oxygen flow. Key Benefits & Intended Impact • Zero-Latency Survival: Eliminates the life-threatening risk of 20-minute one-way communication delays during Lunar (Artemis) and Martian missions. • Proactive Prevention: Shifts space medicine from reactive emergency alarms to early predictive intervention, reducing crew cognitive load. • Dual-Use Earth Spin-Off: Beyond spaceflight, P.U.L.S.E. is directly adaptable for wildland firefighters, underground miners, deep-sea divers, and remote Arctic telemedicine, protecting workers in extreme, disconnected environments. Tools, Languages & Technologies Used • Software & Prototyping: React, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide Icons were used to build our interactive Lunar Mission Control & HUD web prototype. • AI & Data Architecture: Time-series anomaly detection algorithms (LSTM concepts) and multi-sensor fusion logic calibrated using open datasets from NASA OSDR and NASA LSDA. • Target Hardware Concept: Low-power Edge AI microcontrollers, smart conductive textiles, PPG optical sensors, and microfluidic sweat analyzers integrated with spacesuit ECLSS APIs. Creativity & Innovation Traditional telemetry systems only display raw numbers or trigger alarms after dangerous thresholds are crossed—when an astronaut may already be impaired. P.U.L.S.E. is creative because it removes the human bottleneck in acute emergencies through a Closed-Loop Bio-Suit Architecture, pairing a personalized "Digital Twin" of each astronaut with direct hardware actuation. Key Factors Considered by Our Team • False-Positive Prevention: We implemented multi-sensor fusion so a single faulty skin sensor will not trigger unnecessary emergency cooling unless corroborated by heart rate, respiration, and suit CO₂ metrics. • Power & Compute Constraints: Heavy neural network training occurs on Earth using NASA archives, while only a lightweight, compressed inference model runs inside the suit to conserve battery life. • Human Factors & UX: Designed a calm, minimalist helmet HUD and voice alert system to prevent panic and minimize cognitive overload during high-stress EVAs.
